definition: Instructive means serving to teach, inform, or provide useful insight.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word instructive. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know instructive should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The failed launch proved more instructive than a dozen successes, exposing three design flaws in one afternoon.
Informative is weaker than instructive: informative material supplies facts, while instructive material teaches you something you can actually use.
Revelatory is stronger than instructive — a revelatory experience transforms how you see the whole subject, while an instructive one adds a solid, usable lesson.

Educational means providing knowledge or training in a broad, organized way — a curriculum, a museum wing, a term of lectures. Instructive is smaller and more pointed: a single case, mistake, or example that teaches you something you can use. A semester is educational; one well-labeled failure is instructive.

Illuminating means shedding light — an illuminating remark makes something suddenly easier to understand. Instructive goes one step further into practice: it not only clarifies but teaches a usable lesson. An illuminating diagram shows how the engine works; an instructive one shows how to fix it.

The museum's most popular exhibit is a wall of broken pots.
Each shard is labeled with what went wrong: fired too fast, glazed too thick, cooled unevenly.
Visiting potters linger there longer than at the flawless masterpieces two rooms over.
'The perfect pieces are beautiful,' the curator explains, 'but the broken ones are instructive — every crack teaches you something you can use tomorrow.'
Each labeled crack teaches a usable lesson — the broken pots serve to inform and improve the visitor's own craft, which is exactly what instructive means.
neutral; broadly approving

Every trainee pilot at the harbor reads the same forty-page report before touching a wheel: the 1987 grounding of the freighter Alcyone.
Nothing about the file is entertaining, and most of its facts are long obsolete.
It has stayed on the syllabus because it is instructive in a way no textbook chapter manages.
The report reconstructs, minute by minute, how three small, reasonable-looking decisions stacked into a disaster, and trainees finish it able to name the moment they would have turned back.
One old wreck, read closely, teaches the harbor's hardest lesson better than a season of drills.
